P0189.title: Attempt on Brown-measure convergence from general strong convergence

Normalized word traces are checked directly. The determinant calculation independently checks nilpotency. Full proof and all source dependencies are in the proof packet. P0189.title: Weyl equidistribution and unique ergodicity of irrational rotations
P0189.body:
Let alpha be irrational and let R_alpha(x) = x + alpha modulo 1 on the circle. Then R_alpha is UNIQUELY ERGODIC: Lebesgue measure is its only invariant Borel probability measure. Equivalently (Weyl), for every continuous f the Birkhoff averages (1/N) sum_{n=0}^{N-1} f(x + n alpha) converge to the integral of f UNIFORMLY in x, and for every arc I the orbit spends asymptotically |I| of its time in I, for EVERY starting point with no exceptional set. For rational alpha the rotation is periodic and has many invariant measures, so irrationality is exactly what is used.
alpha irrational.
The conclusion for every point (not merely almost every point) is the force of unique ergodicity;
Birkhoff's theorem alone would give an almost-everywhere statement.
Uniform convergence is asserted for CONTINUOUS f - for an indicator it follows by approximating the arc from inside and outside, since the boundary has measure zero.

metadata.proof_text: Let mu be invariant. Its Fourier coefficients satisfy mu-hat(n) = e(n alpha) mu-hat(n) for every integer n, where e(t) = exp(2 pi i t). Since alpha is irrational, e(n alpha) is not 1 for n nonzero, forcing mu-hat(n) = 0 for all n nonzero; a probability measure with all nonzero Fourier coefficients vanishing is Lebesgue measure. Unique ergodicity then gives uniform convergence of Birkhoff averages of continuous functions by the standard equivalence.

P0390.title: Attempt on Hyperuniformity transition in stationary ARW wake states
P0390.body:
ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Conservation, explicit coupling reduction, exact law comparison or spectral calculation Result: Every wake-chain state has the same total k. On a cycle, the complement-of-one-site window therefore has variance rho_N*(1-rho_N)<=1/4 under the unique stationary law, where rho_N=k/N; the whole torus has variance zero. More generally, translation invariance forces sum_y Cov(I_x,I_y)=Cov(I_x,k)=0, but this finite-volume cancellation does not imply mesoscopic hyperuniformity. For comparison, uniform k-subsets have Var(S_B)=|B|*rho_N*(1-rho_N)*(N-|B|)/(N-1), which is volume order for |B|=o(N). Check: Under the uniform k-subset comparison law, E I_x=k/N and E I_x I_y=k*(k-1)/(N*(N-1)); substitution yields the displayed variance. C0100.title: Attempt on Convergence of height-fraction statistics in the sandpile scaling limit
C0100.body:
ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Use the Apollonian structure of the limit to predict the local statistics in each patch. Result: The Pegden-Smart limit is a piecewise-quadratic function whose Hessian takes values in the set Gamma of integer superharmonic matrices; inside a patch where the Hessian is a fixed matrix A in Gamma, the sandpile is (Levine-Pegden-Smart) a periodic pattern determined by A, so the height-j fraction in a patch converges to the frequency of height j in that periodic pattern, which is a computable rational number. Hence the refinement holds in the interior of every patch; the question reduces to the boundary set between patches (the Apollonian gasket of patch boundaries), which has Lebesgue measure zero in the limit but whose discrete neighbourhood might carry a positive fraction of sites at scale n if the boundary layers have width of order n^{alpha}, alpha > 0... the patches are of all sizes (Apollonian), and the total area of patches of diameter < eps tends to zero as eps -> 0 (the gasket has Hausdorff dimension < 2), so for any delta the fraction of sites within the small patches is < delta for eps small, and within large patches the convergence holds; therefore the height-j fraction converges PROVIDED the discrete configuration inside a large patch is exactly the periodic pattern except in a boundary layer of o(n) width, which is the content of the Levine-Pegden-Smart 'Apollonian structure in the abelian sandpile' theorem (they prove the patterns appear; the width of the transition layers is what I could not confirm from memory). Conditional resolution recorded: the height-fraction convergence follows from the patch-pattern theorem plus an o(n) transition-layer bound plus the measure-zero gasket; the identity-element scaling limit remains open beyond the Caracciolo-Paoletti-Sportiello special case. Key identity: Inside a patch with Hessian A the height-j frequency is the frequency of j in the A-pattern; the gasket of boundaries has area zero, so convergence reduces to o(n) transition layers. Obstruction: Transition-layer width between patches not confirmed; identity element limit open.
Refers to the open problem node open-problem-c0100-convergence-of-height-fraction-statistics-in-the-sandpile-scaling-limi
No independent review; result status attempted_unsolved

P0031.body:

Method: Sparse exceptional hitting-time clock estimate Result: For a standard Brownian first hitting time tau of -1, reflection gives P(tau>t)=2 Phi(1/sqrt(t))-1 ~ sqrt(2/pi)t^(-1/2), hence E tau=infinity. P0242.title: Attempt on Optimal stationary stopping under Markov-chain lumping
P0242.body:
ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Optimal stationary stopping under Markov-chain lumping structural calculation Result: For a genuinely lumpable partition, the K=1 inequality follows directly. Start the fine chain in any state of a chosen coarse block and use a fine-chain stopping time attaining stationarity. Its projection has the coarse-chain path law. Any extra fine information can be represented by auxiliary conditional randomness in the coarse filtration, so this yields a randomized coarse stopping rule with stationary terminal law and the same expected duration. Taking maxima proves the claim in this special case. Check: Equivalently disintegrate the stopped fine path given each successively observed coarse path; the conditional continuation probabilities give an adapted randomized coarse stopping rule. The conclusion requires strong lumpability, because otherwise the projected fine path is not the Markov chain defined by stationary-flow matching. Obstruction: For arbitrary partitions, equality of one-step stationary flows does not identify multi-step path laws. The stopping-time projection argument therefore fails at its first premise. A full comparison needs a different potential-theoretic argument and the later lifting result must be reconciled.
Refers to the open problem node open-problem-p0242-optimal-stationary-stopping-under-markov-chain-lumping

C0011.title: Attempt on Scaling limit of local-time level sets of planar random walk in the full range of eta
C0011.body:
ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Second Ray-Knight isomorphism to transfer the DGFF level-set result to local times. Result: By the second Ray-Knight theorem the local time at level theta of the walk is, in law, (1/2)(h + sqrt(2 theta ...))^2 for an independent DGFF-type field h; level sets of the local time at height eta times the cover-time scale correspond to DGFF level sets at height lambda log N with lambda determined by eta and theta, giving eta < 1 + (1/2) sqrt(theta)... in the notation of the notes exactly the range where the corresponding DGFF lambda is below 1. The transfer is rigorous for the part of the level set where the sign of h + constant is positive; the difficulty is the negative branch, where the square masks the sign and the point measures of the two branches are dependent. For eta near the upper endpoint the negative branch contributes a lower-order but not negligible set; separating it needs a joint limit of the two branches, which is again Problem 16.1 in disguise. Obstruction: Sign ambiguity in the isomorphism couples two DGFF level sets; no joint limit is available.

C0011.title: Technique: Second Ray-Knight Isomorphism
C0011.body:
TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). Generalised second Ray-Knight theorem (Eisenbaum, Kaspi, Marcus, Rosen and Shi, 2000): let X be a recurrent symmetric Markov process on a countable state space (for instance continuous-time random walk on a finite connected graph, or on Z^2), started at a base point o, and let tau(u) be the inverse local time at o, the first time the local time at o reaches u. Let (phi_x) be the Gaussian free field on the state space with covariance the Green function of X killed at o, independent of X. Then the field (L^{tau(u)}_x + (1/2) phi_x^2)_x has the same law as ((1/2)(phi_x + sqrt(2u))^2)_x. Dynkin-type isomorphisms exist for transient processes killed at an independent exponential time (there the shift is absent). Uses: transfer of DGFF extremal results to local-time level sets and cover times (Ding-Lee-Peres via the Gaussian free field maximum), thick points of random walk, and the Sabot-Tarres and Lupu loop-soup couplings. Limits: the isomorphism identifies laws, not couplings, of the two sides unless the stronger Lupu coupling is used; the sign of phi is lost in the square, so events about level sets of the local time correspond to two-sided level sets of phi + sqrt(2u). Typical failure: Using the generalized second Ray-Knight isomorphism but omitting or misplacing the additive shift sqrt(2T) term that appears when T is a fixed constant rather than an inverse-local-time stopping time, as in the classical Brownian motion Ray-Knight theorems; dropping or mislocating this shift silently changes which boundary or starting condition the isomorphism is actually describing. Canonical reference: Ray, 1963, Illinois Journal of Mathematics; Knight, 1963, Transactions of the American Mathematical Society; Eisenbaum, Kaspi, Marcus, Rosen and Shi, 2000, Annals of Probability; Lupu, 2016, Annals of Probability.
Recurrent symmetric Markov process; base point o; inverse local time at o
GFF with covariance the Green function of the process killed at o, independent of the process
Identity in law, not a pathwise coupling

C0105.title: Attempt on Multiscale decomposition of the actual zeta function with self-similar increments
C0105.body:
ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Analyse the covariance of the dyadic prime-block increments and the failure of independence. Result: The increments Y_h(l) = sum over primes with log p in (2^{l-1}, 2^l] of Re(p^{-i(tau+h)}) p^{-1/2} have, for tau uniform on [0,T], exact joint moments given by counting solutions of multiplicative equations among primes (Montgomery-Vaughan), so their joint law is asymptotically that of independent uniform phases as long as the number of primes involved is o(log T / log log T) in the moment order; this gives asymptotic independence of any FIXED number of increments at fixed moment order, but the branching-random-walk machinery needs exponential moments of sums of all n = log log T increments simultaneously, i.e. moments of order growing with n, where the multiplicative counting develops correlations from products of primes exceeding T. The dichotomy (50) for the covariance holds exactly for the random model and up to O(1/log T) errors for zeta by the prime number theorem in short intervals. So the decomposition EXISTS with the right covariance structure; what fails is independence at high moment order, precisely for the finest 1/log log T fraction of scales. Reduction: the structural question is equivalent to controlling exponential moments of the full prime sum truncated at T^{1-eps} (which is the ABR approach for the upper bound) and separately handling the last block, and the honest status is that the decomposition is available for all but the last O(1) scales, which is why the O(1) term (C0103) is where the difficulty concentrates. Key identity: Fixed-order joint moments of dyadic prime blocks match independent phases; the failure is at moment order growing with the number of scales. Obstruction: High-moment dependence of the last blocks.

C0153.title: Technique: Local Weak Convergence and the Objective Method
C0153.body:
TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For a sequence of finite, possibly random, rooted graphs G_n, local weak (Benjamini-Schramm) convergence means that for every finite radius r, the distribution of the isomorphism class of the r-ball around the (uniformly, or otherwise canonically) chosen root converges weakly to that of a limiting, typically infinite, random rooted graph (G*, o). The objective method, due to Aldous and Steele, is the broader program of analyzing this limiting infinite object directly, such as a Poisson weighted infinite tree or a unimodular Galton-Watson tree, to compute limiting constants for combinatorial optimization functionals on the finite graphs, such as the minimum spanning tree constant or the limiting value in the random assignment problem, by solving a recursive distributional (fixed-point) equation on the infinite limit rather than working with finite-n computations directly. It does not by itself establish that a given sequence converges locally weakly, which typically must be separately verified via a subsequential compactness argument together with uniqueness of subsequential limits, and it does not directly give convergence of global, extensive functionals without an additional concentration or summation argument beyond the purely local statement. Typical failure: Assuming that local weak convergence of the underlying random graph automatically implies convergence of a global extensive functional, such as the total weight of a minimum spanning tree, at the same per-vertex limiting rate; local convergence controls only typical local neighborhoods, and passing to a global average requires an additional uniform-integrability or concentration argument, often the genuinely hard part of an objective-method proof, which is easy to overlook once the local limit has been identified. Canonical reference: Benjamini and Schramm, 2001, Electronic Journal of Probability; Aldous and Steele, 2004, in Probability on Discrete Structures, Springer; Aldous and Lyons, 2007, Electronic Journal of Probability.
a sequence of (random) rooted graphs with controlled local neighborhoods, such as bounded degree, sufficient for tightness
existence of a limiting infinite, typically unimodular, random rooted graph as the local weak limit
the functional of interest is expressible as, or well approximated by, a sum or average of local, root-based quantities
for extensive functionals: an additional argument, such as subadditivity or concentration, to pass from the local limit to a law of large numbers for the global sum
